body:
What the 3 movements had in common

The Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj and Arya Samaj emerged during the 19th century and sought to change religious and social life. All three criticised aspects of image worship and excessive ritualism. They also associated religious improvement with concerns such as women's education, caste restrictions and social customs.

These similarities can make statements about the movements appear interchangeable. The most useful way to distinguish them is to identify their founders, founding places, religious sources of authority and characteristic methods.

Core comparison

MovementFoundationReligious emphasisCharacteristic approach
Brahmo SamajRaja Rammohun Roy; Brahmo Sabha, Calcutta, 1828Monotheism; Upanishadic ideas; reason and moral judgmentReligious reinterpretation, public debate and social reform
Prarthana SamajAtmaram Pandurang; Bombay, 1867One formless God; prayer; Maharashtra Bhakti traditionPrayer meetings, caste reform, women's education and widow remarriage
Arya SamajDayanand Saraswati; Bombay, 1875Supreme, infallible authority of the Vedas; one GodVedic revival, social reform, Shuddhi and educational institutions

The decisive doctrinal distinction

All three movements supported monotheistic religious ideas, but they did not treat scripture in the same way.

  • Brahmo approach: Rammohun Roy drew upon the Upanishads and relied upon reason and ethical judgment in examining religious practices.
  • Prarthana approach: Members drew upon the devotional teachings of saints such as Namdev and Tukaram and did not accept one book as the wholly infallible word of God.
  • Arya approach: Dayanand maintained that the Vedas were the supreme and infallible religious authority when correctly interpreted.

Therefore, a statement that all three movements rejected image worship may be broadly consistent with their reformist teachings. A statement that all three regarded the Vedas as infallible is incorrect.

Founders, influences and later leaders

Questions about founders require particular care. Keshab Chandra Sen influenced the Prarthana Samaj, but it was founded by Atmaram Pandurang. Similarly, M. G. Ranade and R. G. Bhandarkar were major leaders associated with Prarthana Samaj, not replacements for its founding name.

Within the Brahmo movement, Debendranath Tagore strengthened the organisation after Roy's death. The 1866 split produced the Adi Brahmo Samaj and Brahmo Samaj of India. The 1878 Sadharan Brahmo Samaj was a later development, not another name for the 1866 division.

Within the Arya Samaj, Lala Hansraj is associated with DAV education at Lahore, while Munshi Ram or Swami Shraddhanand is associated with Gurukul Kangri.

The Gujarat facts to retain

Two different Gujarat connections are especially important. Dayanand Saraswati was born at Tankara in 1824, although he founded Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875. Separately, the Manav Dharma Sabha was established at Surat in 1844, before the Prarthana Samaj was founded in Bombay in 1867. The Prarthana Samaj subsequently established branches at Surat and Ahmedabad.

Chronology of the principal developments

The sequence begins with Atmiya Sabha in 1815 and the Brahmo Sabha in 1828. The Brahmo movement later developed through the Tattwabodhini Sabha in 1839, the 1866 division and the establishment of the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj in 1878.

In western India, the Manav Dharma Sabha appeared at Surat in 1844 and the Prarthana Samaj at Bombay in 1867. The Arya Samaj began in Bombay in 1875, followed by major educational developments including the DAV school at Lahore in 1886 and Gurukul Kangri in 1902.

Common factual distinctions

  • 1829 and 1856: The former concerns the prohibition of sati under Bentinck; the latter concerns Hindu widow remarriage and is especially associated with Vidyasagar.
  • 1828 and 1867: The former marks the Brahmo Sabha in Calcutta; the latter marks the Prarthana Samaj in Bombay.
  • 1867 and 1875: Prarthana Samaj preceded Arya Samaj.
  • Tankara and Bombay: Tankara was Dayanand's birthplace; Bombay was the founding place of Arya Samaj.
  • Shuddhi and DAV: Shuddhi was a reconversion practice; DAV refers to an educational approach and institutions.

These distinctions reveal how one broad period of reform contained several different religious and organisational approaches. The movements are connected by common social concerns, but their doctrines, founders and institutions must be remembered separately.

Prelims focus

  • Brahmo Sabha: Rammohun Roy, Calcutta, 1828.
  • Prarthana Samaj: Atmaram Pandurang, Bombay, 1867.
  • Arya Samaj: Dayanand Saraswati, Bombay, 1875.
  • Adi Brahmo Samaj and Brahmo Samaj of India: division of 1866.
  • Sadharan Brahmo Samaj: 1878; DAV school, Lahore: 1886; Gurukul Kangri: 1902.
  • Trap: Shared criticism of idolatry does not imply identical beliefs about Vedic authority.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 95–100; National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), lesson 18, Social Changes in Modern India, printed pp. 30–34; Brahmo Samaj, Brief History of the Brahmo Samaj, consulted 20 November 2026; Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Mumbai Legacy Project: Prarthana Samaj, pp. 1–2, consulted 20 November 2026; Vanya Vaidehi Bhargav, Arya Samaj, Oxford Bibliographies in Hinduism, Introduction, published 7 January 2025, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Comparing Brahmo, Prarthana and Arya Samaj for Prelims
